learning_objective: 🎯 Master the fundamentals of electrostatics by understanding how electric charges interact, the invisible fields they create, and how to calculate these forces using Coulomb's and Gauss's laws!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Charge is a fundamental property of matter. Like charges repel, and unlike charges attract. Charges are always conserved (can't be created or destroyed) and quantized, meaning any charge $q$ is an integral multiple of the basic electron charge ($q = ne$).

This law calculates the electrostatic force between two point charges. The force is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Formula: $F = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$.

An electric field is the region around a charge where its force can be felt by other charges. We visualize this using Electric Field Lines, which start at positive charges and end at negative charges. Remember: Two field lines never cross each other!

An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance. It has a 'Dipole Moment' directed from the negative to the positive charge. When placed in a uniform electric field, a dipole experiences a turning force called torque.

Electric Flux is a measure of the number of electric field lines passing through a surface. Gauss's Law states that the total electric flux through any closed imaginary surface (Gaussian surface) is equal to $1/\epsilon_0$ times the total net charge enclosed by that surface.

fun_activity.title: 🎈 The Magic Balloon Experiment
fun_activity.instructions: Rub a rubber balloon or a plastic comb on dry hair for a few seconds. Bring it close to tiny pieces of paper on a table. Watch the paper jump up and stick to the object! This proves charging by friction and electrostatic attraction in real life.

exam_tips: 📌 Always define your 'Gaussian surface' clearly and draw the diagram when deriving electric fields for wires, sheets, or spheres. Examiners look for the diagram for step marks!
📌 Don't forget the vector notation! Force and Electric Field are vectors. Always specify the direction alongside the magnitude in your final answer.
📌 Remember the constants: The value of $1/(4\pi\epsilon_0)$ is strictly $9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2/\text{C}^2$ in a vacuum.
quick_recap: ⭐ Like charges repel, unlike charges attract; charge is always conserved and strictly quantized.
⭐ Coulomb's Law gives the force between point charges, while the Electric Field gives the force experienced per unit charge.
⭐ Gauss's Law is the ultimate shortcut for finding electric fields of symmetric, continuous charge distributions!
